note: The English teen edition quotes the KJV in each chapter's epigraph; every French epigraph is the whole verse(s) verbatim from Louis Segond (1910), with the “(KJV)” label dropped and only French typographic spacing added. Psalm 68:5 and Psalm 62:8 (English numbering) are Psaume 68:6 and 62:9 in Segond and are cited that way in the text; the Psalm 62 epigraph stops before Segond's closing “— Pause” (Selah), ending « Dieu est notre refuge. »

In-body quotations marked mined are Segond word for word (partial verses). Lamentations 3:26 in Segond has no word for KJV's “hope”, so ch. 3 quotes « Il est bon d’attendre en silence » and the study question talks of « attendre en silence »; Psalm 16:6's “goodly heritage” becomes Segond's « héritage délicieux » (chapter 1 title too). All other echoes (living sacrifice, grain of wheat, earthen vessels as « vases de terre », everlasting love/arms, carried to grey hair) are self_rendered.

Names, places and terms follow elisabeth-elliot-a-life-children.fr (les Waorani, les Quichuas/le quichua, les Colorados, Shandia, Arajuno, Palm Beach, la Tiwaeno, Gikari = « pic-vert », « Doe the nexte thynge » kept in old English with the gloss « Fais la chose suivante »). Jim Elliot's 1949 sentence is quoted as in Brave for God Book Three fr: « Il n’est pas fou, celui qui donne ce qu’il ne peut garder pour gagner ce qu’il ne peut perdre. »

Her books keep their English titles in italics with a literal French gloss in guillemets the first time (Through Gates of Splendor, These Strange Ashes, No Graven Image, The Savage My Kinsman, Let Me Be a Woman, Passion and Purity, Gateway to Joy, Amy Carmichael's If); a reviewer may prefer published French titles where they exist.
